scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Change-management ticket #9139: Hello, after last night's maintenance
somewhere in the middle of the network, people are saying the two halves
can't see each other any more -- machines with the 20.x numbers and machines
with the 120.x numbers supposedly can't reach across at all. I was told the
two halves "speak different routing languages" and something in the middle
translates between them -- that's honestly all I understood. Could someone
check whether the two halves are still talking and fix whatever joins them?
Thanks!

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected; the
  lab runs at its healthy baseline. The claimed SPLIT does not exist: PC0
  (20.1.1.10, OSPF side) reaches PC12 (120.1.1.10, EIGRP side) end to end with 0%
  loss in both directions. EIGRP -> OSPF redistribution is live (EIGRP prefixes
  112.x/103.x/120.x appear in the OSPF RIB). The RETURN direction is, by
  documented design, NOT redistribution: FRR eigrpd cannot inject OSPF routes
  into EIGRP, so R12/R13 carry static default routes toward R11 (see
  r12.startup/r13.startup + r11 frr.conf comments). The correct answer is
  is_anomaly=false. This case measures over-diagnosis of a split that is not
  present (cf. kath5-r11-redistribute-eigrp-missing, where it IS).

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario. No fault was injected; the
network is at healthy baseline. The reported symptom -- the OSPF and EIGRP
halves are split into isolated islands -- is NOT reproducible. Decisively, PC0
(20.1.1.10) on the OSPF side reaches PC12 (120.1.1.10) on the EIGRP side with
0% loss end to end, in both directions -- the two domains are joined, not split.

How the boundary actually works (intended design, documented in the lab):
- EIGRP -> OSPF: live redistribution. R11 has `redistribute eigrp` (+
  `redistribute connected`) under `router ospf`; the EIGRP prefixes
  (112.x/103.x/120.x) are present in the OSPF RIB on the backbone.
- OSPF -> EIGRP: NOT redistribution. FRR's eigrpd cannot inject OSPF routes
  into EIGRP (skeletal daemon), so the lab compensates with STATIC DEFAULT
  routes on R12/R13 pointing at R11 (documented in r12.startup, r13.startup,
  and r11's frr.conf). The EIGRP-side routers reach the OSPF side via those
  defaults BY DESIGN.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: the split the ticket claims does not
exist and the user's report cannot be confirmed. A correct agent reproduces the
cross-domain PC0<->PC12 path (working) and reports no fault. Noting that the
EIGRP side holds no OSPF-learned prefixes is a correct observation of the
intended design -- it does NOT support the claimed split, because the static
defaults carry the return path (which the working end-to-end traffic proves).
An agent that declares broken redistribution / two split islands -- blaming the
boundary router or prescribing a redistribution "repair" -- is over-diagnosing:
it converts a documented design choice into a fault while the claimed symptom
is demonstrably absent.

agent.diagnosis_text:
End-to-end reachability between the 20.x and 120.x sides is currently healthy. From the edge hosts, 20.1.1.10 (pc0) and 120.1.1.10 (pc12) can ping each other bidirectionally with 0% loss and ~1 ms RTT. The “translator in the middle” is r11, which is running both protocols and redistributing between them. Evidence: r11 has active OSPF adjacencies on 111.1.1.0/8 (to r1) and EIGRP neighbors on 112.1.1.0/8 (to r12) and 103.1.1.0/8 (to r13). Its OSPF config redistributes EIGRP, so the OSPF side learns 120/8; r1 indeed has an OSPF route to 120.0.0.0/8 via r11 (111.1.1.2). On the return path, r12 (EIGRP side) uses a kernel default route via 112.1.1.1 (r11), confirmed by “K>* 0.0.0.0/0 via 112.1.1.1” in its routing table, which ensures packets to 20/8 reach r11 for onward OSPF forwarding.

Mechanistically, this matches a functioning OSPF↔EIGRP handoff: EIGRP-learned 120/8 is injected into OSPF by r11, and the EIGRP domain returns traffic using a default route to r11. Localization: r11 (EE/B segments) is the redistribution point; r1 carries the OSPF side; r12 carries the EIGRP side.

Root cause: No current fault detected; any outage likely coincided with the reported maintenance but has since cleared.

Corrective fix: No action required now. As a hardening step, consider adding “redistribute ospf” under EIGRP on r11 so the EIGRP side learns explicit OSPF prefixes (not only relying on a default), and add monitoring for r11’s OSPF/EIGRP neighbor states to catch transient issues.

per_axis.axis: bonus-notes-baseline-healthy: notes PC0 reaches PC12 across the boundary at baseline, EIGRP prefixes are in the OSPF RIB, and (any valid form) that the EIGRP side's return path via static defaults is the lab's intended design rather than a fault
per_axis.rationale: Agent confirmed PC0↔PC12 reachability, showed EIGRP prefixes being redistributed into OSPF, and explained the EIGRP-side default via R11 provides the intended return path rather than a fault.

The investigation log contains direct evidence (host reachability tests, router neighbor and routing outputs) that the two domains are connected and that r11 is performing redistribution; the conclusions follow logically and cover the essential checks to rule out the reported split.
